field.label: Send through this module
field.comment: With this off, Magento sends the way it did before the module was installed. Nothing here is lost, and turning it back on restores it.

field.label: Provider
field.comment: Picking one fills in the server, the port and the encryption, and explains what that provider means by the two credential fields.

field.label: Server
field.comment: A host name, without a scheme. A whole address pasted here is understood and tidied up.

field.label: Port
field.comment: 587 for STARTTLS, 465 for TLS from the first byte. Port 25 is blocked outbound by most hosting companies.

field.label: Encryption
field.comment: This has to match the port. The two together are the commonest reason a correct password looks like a dead server.

field.label: Log in with
field.comment: Leave this alone unless a provider asks for something specific. The health check reports what the server offers.

field.label: Password
field.comment: Stored encrypted with the installation's own key. It is never written to the log, to an alert or to the report.

field.label: Give up after
field.comment: Seconds to wait for the server. Five is enough for any provider in the list; a longer wait only makes a checkout page slower on the day the server is down.

field.label: Check the certificate
field.comment: Leave this on. Turning it off makes an untrusted certificate work, and makes an intercepted connection work too.

group.label: Sender
group.comment: Only needed where the provider insists. A Magento installation has sender addresses in half a dozen settings and in any number of modules, and a provider that only accepts one of them will refuse the rest.

field.label: Always send from
field.comment: Overrides the sender of every message. Leave empty to keep whatever each message already says.

field.label: Send bounces to
field.comment: The envelope sender, which is where undeliverable mail comes back to. A different thing from the address above, and the one providers check.

group.label: Health check
group.comment: The check opens a connection, raises encryption and logs in, then says goodbye without sending anything. It costs the provider nothing and counts against no sending limit — and it proves the connection, never the delivery.

field.label: How often
field.comment: A cron expression. Every quarter of an hour by default, which is about as long as anybody wants to be unable to send without knowing it.

field.label: Reuse a verdict for
field.comment: Seconds. Keeps a dashboard, a cron run and a console command in the same minute from opening three connections to learn the same thing. The button on this page always checks now.

field.label: Failed checks before warning
field.comment: Mail servers have bad minutes. A refused password is reported at once whatever this says, because that will not fix itself.

field.label: Failed messages before warning
field.comment: Real messages that could not be sent. This is the ground truth: a shop whose order confirmations are failing is broken whatever a connection test says.

field.label: Counted within
field.comment: Seconds. Three failures in half an hour is a broken shop; three over a fortnight is three bad addresses.

field.label: Say it again after
field.comment: Seconds of silence before the same problem is reported a second time. Six hours by default: often enough not to be forgotten, rarely enough not to be filtered.

group.label: Sender domain
group.comment: The connection check proves the shop can hand a message to its provider. Whether a receiving server believes that message is decided by what the sending domain publishes in DNS — and that is where "the settings are right and the mail still is not arriving" nearly always ends up.

field.label: Check what the domain publishes
field.comment: Four times a day, on cron, and never while a page is being rendered. It reads SPF, DKIM and DMARC and never changes anything.

group.label: Who is told
group.comment: A problem is reported once, again if its reason changes, and once more after a long silence. When it is over, that is reported too.

field.label: A bar across the admin panel
field.comment: The channel that always works, because somebody logs in to process orders anyway.

field.label: An e-mail
field.comment: Sent through the server's own local mail command rather than the provider, because the provider is what is not working. That makes it a second chance rather than a guarantee: local mail is often unconfigured, and often lands in a spam folder.

field.label: To
field.comment: Empty means the shop's general contact address.

field.label: A webhook
field.comment: For a chat room or a monitoring system. Use this where nobody opens the panel daily.

field.label: Webhook address
field.comment: An https address. A JSON body with a text field is posted to it, which is what Slack, Teams and Discord all accept.

group.label: Log
group.comment: Outgoing mail is customer correspondence: names, addresses, order contents, the occasional password reset link. The defaults keep as little of it as is still useful.

field.label: Keep a log of what was sent
field.comment: Sender, recipients, subject and what the server said. This is what answers "did the customer get it?" without guessing.

field.label: Keep the message body
field.comment: Only for messages that failed, and only while they are within the retention — this is what makes sending them again possible once the settings are fixed. It is also the one setting here that stores whole customer e-mails.

field.label: Keep entries for
field.comment: Days. Entries older than this are deleted nightly, whether the log is switched on or not — a log turned off last month should not still be holding last month's mail.

group.label: Test message
group.comment: The health check proves a connection. Only a real message proves delivery, and only the mailbox it arrives in can say whether it landed in the inbox or the spam folder.

field.label: Send a test message to
field.comment: Empty means the address warnings go to.
